There's also a pattern of unsupported adjacency assumptions: phrases like "CALL RET" being described as "a call followed immediately by a return," or "INC PUSH" as "a counter increment," or "PXOR MOVAPS" as "SIMD register-clearing" — these infer literal instruction adjacency and specific semantic roles that the n-gram features don't necessarily establish, since graph-aware n-grams need not reflect adjacent instructions. Several other claims (generic code-style statistics, common in all x86 binaries, model bias vs. behavior) are reasonably hedged but still speculative beyond what the evidence directly supports.

The SHAP analysis itself seems faithful in terms of sign and magnitude accuracy, with the top feature correctly identified and benign-leaning features correctly noted as sparse, though scoping the claim to "top-20" rather than unqualified is a minor nuance worth flagging.

I'll keep faithful true but flag the overreach claims as unsupported rather than discrepancies—the "only benign-leaning feature" scoping issue and the SHAP-as-bias framing both go into unsupported_claims instead, since direction and magnitude are still correct. Generic domain claims about x86 prevalence don't tie to this specific sample, so I'm skipping those.
